title: A Telegram bot for a business that already has a site
metaTitle: A Telegram bot beside an existing site
excerpt: Use a Telegram bot for a status, a booking ping, or simple intake when the site already explains the offer. The bot should not become a second, thinner website.

faqs.question: What should a Telegram bot do if the business already has a site?
faqs.answer: Use it for a status, a booking ping, or a short intake that a known group should not have to wait on. The site remains the place the offer, the price, and the proof are explained. When someone asks the bot a question the page already answers, reply with the link and the list of real commands.

faqs.question: Who should be allowed to use the commands?
faqs.answer: Start in a private chat or a private group, and decide who may ask for status, who may submit intake, and who may trigger a ping. A status that reveals a customer file in a public room is a leak. Widen a command only when that wider audience is safe.

faqs.question: What should the bot do with a question it does not handle?
faqs.answer: Say that it does not know, and give a way to reach a person. List that edge in the help text next to the real commands. An open chat that improvises refunds, prices, or dates will eventually send a confident wrong reply in the business's voice.

markdown:
A Telegram bot for business is worth adding when the site already explains the offer and a known group still waits on a person for a short list of facts. Use the bot for a job the site should not make someone sit on: a status, a booking ping, a simple intake. The site remains the place the price, the story, and the proof are read.

If the group is not already in Telegram, the bot will not move them there. If the job needs a catalog, a long policy, or a comparison, send them to the page. The bot can carry the link. It should not become a second, worse website.

## The jobs that belong in the chat

Status answers a question people already ask a human. Where is the order. Is the file ready. Did the form arrive. The bot reads a source you trust and replies with the fact and the time it was true. A status that invents a story is worse than a slow human.

A booking ping tells a person that a slot was requested or confirmed. The site, or the calendar behind it, still holds the truth. The bot is the tap on the shoulder. It should name the who and the when, and link to the record. A ping with no link makes someone open three tools to learn what the ping meant.

Intake collects a known set of fields from people who already have the bot: a name, a link, a date, a budget range. One question at a time, then a confirmation of the list, then a write into the place a person will see the same day. Intake is finished when the record exists. Charm is not the acceptance criterion.

Keep the list short enough for a help command that fits on a phone without a manual. Status, ping, intake. If you need a twelfth command, you are building a product, and the product deserves a screen on the site you already maintain.

## The site keeps the explanation

The homepage, the service page, and the product page remain canonical. They have the room to show the work, the price logic, and the limits. A chat thread is a poor room for that reading. When someone asks the bot “what do you charge,” the honest reply is the link to the page that says it, plus one sentence on what the bot can do. Do not paste a stale price into the help text and hope you remember to update both.

This split also keeps search and sharing intact. A page can be cited, forwarded, and updated in one place. A bot transcript cannot. If a fact changes, change it on the site, and let the bot point at the site. Two sources of a price will diverge on a Friday and you will not notice until a customer quotes the wrong one.

Public projects make the division easy to picture. Leadly and Got Next are product interfaces. Trade Moai is a trading interface concept. None of those jobs is a chat command. A bot beside them might tell a teammate that a build finished or that a lead arrived. The interface still does the work the user came to do.

Write the help text in the same voice as the site. Short sentences. The real commands. What each one needs. What it will not do. People should not discover the bot by typing guesses that hit an open model and get a confident wrong answer.

## Who may ask

Start in a private chat or a private group: the client team, the staff channel, the small list of people who already wait on you. Decide who may ask for status, who may submit intake, and who may trigger a ping. A status command that reveals a customer file to a public group is a leak, not an automation.

Widen a command only when the wider audience is safe. A public “what are your hours” command can be public. A public “status of order 1842” cannot. If you cannot separate those permissions, do not ship the status command.

The [W3C’s overview of WCAG 2](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) notes that the guidelines can apply beyond traditional web pages, under principles that include understandable and operable. A bot people must operate should make the actions obvious and the replies plain. A failed command should say what was missing. A successful one should say what was saved. Those two sentences are the interface. A typing indicator with no result is a hang.

Identify the bot as a bot. People in a business group deserve to know a script replied. “This is an automated reply from the studio bot” costs one line and prevents a customer from thinking a person approved a promise.

## What the bot should refuse

Refuse open conversation as a feature. A model that chats will be asked about refunds, legal terms, and discounts, and it will answer some of them. If a question is outside the three commands, say that you do not know and give the human path. The help text should list that edge in the same voice as the commands.

Refuse payments, deletions, and anything a person cannot undo, unless a human confirms a draft first. The first version does not need those commands. A bot that can refund because someone typed a phrase in a busy channel will eventually do it on the wrong order.

Refuse to be the only copy of a record. Telegram is not your database. Write intake to the system you already check, the same place the site’s form writes. If the bot is down, the site still accepts the request, and a person can still see it. A workflow that exists only inside a chat history will vanish the day someone’s phone dies.

Give the bot an owner. Someone watches the first weeks of replies, updates the help text when a command changes, and turns a command off when the source behind it is no longer true. A bot without that person becomes a confident outdated notice. The group mutes it, and then a real ping has nowhere to land.

## A thin build over a boring manual step

Do not automate a status nobody can answer by hand. If “where is the order” requires three people and a spreadsheet with conflicting dates, the bot has nothing reliable to read. Fix the source. Then the command is a window on that source.

Log each command: who asked, what you returned, when. You will need the log the first time a customer says they were told the file was ready. The log is also how you learn which command is used and which one was a guess. Unused commands should be removed so the help text stays true.

Keep secrets out of the chat. Tokens, customer lists, and unreleased work do not belong in a group even a small one, unless you have decided that group is the right audience. The bot should fetch what it needs on request, not paste a dump at the start of the day.

Set hours if the humans have hours. A booking ping at 2 a.m. can wait in the queue and post in the morning, unless the job is truly overnight. Say that in the help text so nobody thinks the ping failed.

Test with the people who will be pinged. If they mute the bot in week one, the notifications are too frequent or too vague. Cut until the ping is something they would have wanted a colleague to tap them for.

## The first week, watched on purpose

Run the bot beside the old habit, not instead of it, for the first week. If intake still arrives by email, keep the email. Compare what the bot recorded with what a person would have written down. Differences are bugs: a missing budget, a link stripped of its query string, a name truncated. Fix those before you tell a client the bot is the way in.

Tell the group the list of commands in one message, then pin it. Invite them to break it. Empty input, a huge link, two requests in one breath. The replies should stay boring. You are looking for sentences you would be willing to leave unread for an hour, because sometimes they will be unread for an hour. A reply that says “saved, and a person will see it today” is safe. A reply that says “you are booked” is not, unless a person has confirmed the book.

Count the pings. More than a handful a day for a small team means the bot is narrating work instead of interrupting for work. Raise the threshold. A booking ping for every calendar change, including the ones staff made themselves, is how the channel becomes a log nobody opens. Ping the events a person must act on. Leave the rest in the record.

When the week is clean, turn off the duplicate path you no longer need, and say so. “New project requests go through the bot or the form. Both write to the same list.” Leaving three doors open forever means one of them will rot, and it will be the one a client still uses.

## When a different room is the right room

Some teams live in Discord, and the same discipline applies with one change: pick a single staff job rather than a tour of the platform. [A Discord bot that does one staff job](/blog/a-discord-bot-that-does-one-staff-job) is the next piece if that is where the work already talks. The site still explains the offer. The bot still does not become the shop.

If a short command list beside an existing site is the shape you need, see [Hanabi’s services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The studio designs and builds that kind of bot when the group, the source of truth, and the jobs are specific.
